title: When Earth Lost the Sun's Shield
hook: The Sun's magnetic bubble shelters Earth from interstellar gas. NASA-funded studies suggest that as the Sun ploughed through dense galactic clouds, that shield shrank — and the climate felt it.
key_points: The heliosphere is the Sun's magnetic bubble, holding back interstellar gas and cosmic rays.
As the Sun orbits the galaxy it passes through dense interstellar clouds that can compress the bubble.
Studies suggest such passages may line up with ancient ice ages on Earth.
A second thread: the young Sun's violent superflares could have warmed the early Earth.
That helps with the 'faint young Sun' puzzle — liquid water when the Sun shone far dimmer.
content_html: Earth does not sit in empty space. It sits inside the heliosphere, the magnetic bubble the solar wind blows against the surrounding interstellar medium. That bubble is not fixed in size: as the Sun carries the planets on its long orbit around the Milky Way, it occasionally ploughs into dense clouds of interstellar gas that squeeze the bubble inward.
extra_html: Two NASA-funded studies, summarised by ScienceDaily, argue that this galactic weather has left marks in Earth's climate record — with the timing of some ancient ice ages potentially matching passages through dense regions of the galaxy. The same work looks at the opposite end of the story: the young Sun's enormous superflares. Those outbursts may have delivered enough energy to help keep early Earth warm enough for liquid water at a time when the Sun itself was much dimmer than today, one of the longest-standing puzzles in planetary science. Both are claims about correlation and mechanism rather than settled history, but they connect our planet's habitability to where the Solar System happened to be in the galaxy.

related.title: What Powers the Sun
related.hook: The Sun isn't burning like a fire — it's fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, and a sliver of mass turning into pure energy is what lights up our sky.

related.title: The Sun's 'Switch-Off' Signal That Forecasts the Next Cycle
related.hook: Partway through the Sun's 11-year cycle, a 'switch-off' moment shuts down its most violent storms — and the sunspots left over forecast the next cycle's strength years in advance.

related.title: The Sun Is Covered in Whirlpools Too Small to See Until Now
related.hook: Astronomers found plasma vortices on the Sun just 20 kilometres across — small enough to have hidden in plain sight, and possibly the engines behind its smallest flares.

related.title: The universe's most energetic particles come from nearby
related.hook: Match the sky map of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays against catalogues of galaxies and the signal snaps into focus at one distance: everything within about 60 megaparsecs.

flashcards.prompt: What is the heliosphere, and what does it do for Earth?
flashcards.back_html: The Sun's magnetic bubble, inflated by the solar wind. It holds back interstellar gas and deflects much of the incoming cosmic-ray flux.

flashcards.prompt: What is the 'faint young Sun' puzzle these studies bear on?

choices.text: The early Sun was much dimmer, yet early Earth still had liquid water
The early Sun was brighter, so Earth should have boiled away
The Sun's colour has shifted from red to yellow over time

flashcards.explanation_html: A dimmer young Sun should have left Earth frozen. The studies suggest the young Sun's superflares delivered extra energy, helping keep the early planet warm enough for water.

flashcards.prompt: How could the Sun's path through the galaxy affect Earth's climate?
flashcards.back_html: Passing through a dense interstellar cloud can compress the heliosphere, changing what reaches Earth — a possible trigger the studies link to ancient ice ages.
